Jointly Optimizing Memory, Computing and
Ofﬂoading for Energy-Efﬁcient DNN Inference
Yunchu Han, Graduate Student Member, IEEE, Zhaojun Nan, Member, IEEE,
Sheng Zhou, Senior Member, IEEE, and Zhisheng Niu, Fellow, IEEE
Abstract—In edge intelligence systems, computation ofﬂoading
and dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) are widely
used to improve energy efﬁciency. However, as applications like
deep neural network (DNN) inference evolve in complexity, their
demands for memory resources have progressively increased,
establishing memory as a critical bottleneck that impacts both
latency and energy consumption. In this paper, we propose a
joint optimization scheme integrating memory, computing and
ofﬂoading for energy-efﬁcient DNN inference. We formulate
the energy minimization problem under deadline constraints
as a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem,
where the main challenge arises from the coupling between
ofﬂoading and resource optimization. To address this issue, we
decompose the original problem into two subproblems under a
ﬁxed ofﬂoading policy. The local subproblem is transformed into
an equivalent geometric programming (GP) problem to derive the
optimal memory frequency and computing frequency, while the
edge subproblem is solved via convex optimization. An efﬁcient
coordinate descent (CD) algorithm is further developed to jointly
optimize all variables. Simulation results demonstrate that our
proposed algorithm achieves near-optimal performance with the
gap from the optimal policy being at most 9.3%, and reduces the
energy consumption of devices by up to 16.1% compared with
benchmarks without memory frequency optimization.
Index
Terms—Edge
intelligence,
DNN
inference,
energy-
efﬁcient, memory frequency, computing frequency.
I. INTRODUCTION
I
N the era of artiﬁcial intelligence (AI), deep neural net-
works (DNNs) have been extensively deployed on mobile
devices for different applications, such as image recognition
[2], object detection [3], AI-generated content (AIGC) services
[4], etc. However, DNN inference usually requires substantial
computation and memory access costs, leading to intolerable
latency and enormous energy consumption. For example,
using MobileNetv1 SSD for object detection on smartphones
consumes over 20% of the total energy consumption [5]. The
inference process of the transformer-based language model
produces an extremely high carbon emission footprint, which
is even higher than that of training [6]. The model loading
time of ResNet50 on OPPO R17 is about 1 second, while the

niuzhs@tsinghua.edu.cn).

Chongqing Polytechnic University of Electronic Technology, Chongqing
401331, China (e-mail: nanzhaojun@cquet.edu.cn).
An earlier version of this paper has been published in IEEE GLOBECOM
2025 [1].
inference time is about 1.3 seconds [7]. Therefore, it is signif-
icantly challenging to achieve real-time and energy-efﬁcient
DNN inference, especially on resource-limited devices.
To address these challenges, wireless edge intelligence [8],
[9] has been proposed as a new paradigm, where mobile
devices can ofﬂoad their computational tasks to the edge
node (e.g., base station, roadside unit) with the mobile edge
computing (MEC) server so that the resource costs for de-
vices can be reduced. In addition, the dynamic voltage and
frequency scaling (DVFS) technique [10], [11] is widely
applied to balance the latency and energy consumption by
adjusting the frequency of processors (e.g., CPU frequency,
GPU frequency). Combining these techniques, existing work
has considered the joint optimization of computing resources
and ofﬂoading to reduce the energy consumption of mobile
devices from various perspectives (e.g., batch processing [12],
robust optimization [13], integrated sensing-communication-
computation [14]) and scenarios (e.g., Internet of Things
(IoT) [15], vehicular network [16], unmanned aerial vehicle
(UAV) [17]). However, the above studies solely consider the
joint optimization of computing and communication resources
while neglecting the optimization of memory resources, which
can signiﬁcantly impact the latency and energy consumption
of DNN inference [18], [19].
The demands for memory resources of DNNs have dramat-
ically increased due to the proliferation of model parameters
and the large volume of intermediate data. Memory resource
optimization includes various approaches, such as memory
footprint management and memory frequency adjustment.
Many studies have focused on the memory footprint man-
agement with different methods (e.g., dynamic allocation of
memory size for DNN inference [20], efﬁcient DNN block
swapping to reduce the unnecessary memory copying and
processing [21], slicing and preload-aware memory planning
to balance the latency and memory usage [22]). In fact, DNN
inference is increasingly constrained by the memory wall
[23], where the processing speed of computing units is often
limited by the rate at which data is accessed from memory.
Therefore, memory frequency has become a critical factor
that impacts the inference time. Recently, a few studies have
investigated the memory frequency adjustment [24], [25]. In
[24], the authors observe that increasing the memory frequency
can accelerate some GPU kernels. In [25], it is observed
that the adjustment of memory frequency can improve the
performance of DNN inference on GPUs (i.e., latency per
unit of energy consumption). However, the impact of jointly
adjusting memory frequency and computing frequency on

DNN inference time has not been well-understood.
To further investigate the impact of memory frequency and
computing frequency on DNN inference time, we measure the
average inference time of four representative DNN models on
the CIFAR-100 dataset [26] using two different devices with
different frequency settings, as shown in Fig. 1. Increasing
the memory frequency from 0.102 GHz to 1.6 GHz on Jetson
TX1 reduces the inference time of DenseNet121 [27] and
ResNet152 [28] by 72% and 83%, respectively, which is con-
siderably greater than the improvement achieved by increasing
the computing frequency. A similar trend is observed on Jetson
Xavier NX, where adjusting the memory frequency from 0.204
GHz to 1.6 GHz improves the inference time of VGG19 [29]
and ViT-B/16 [30] by 74% and 67%, respectively. In fact,
the impact of memory frequency and computing frequency on
the inference time varies for different DNN models, reﬂecting
their various computational and memory access costs. There-
fore, jointly adjusting the memory frequency and computing
frequency can provide more opportunities to reduce the energy
consumption of DNN inference.
In this paper, we investigate energy-efﬁcient DNN inference
in a multi-device edge intelligence system from a memory-
computing-communication co-optimization perspective. Un-
like most existing MEC-based studies that mainly optimize
computing and communication resources, we explicitly con-
sider the memory frequency of mobile devices as a controllable
resource. For local inference, the memory frequency and
computing frequency are jointly optimized to minimize the
energy consumption. For edge inference, the uplink bandwidth
allocation is optimized to minimize the energy consumption
of transmission. Considering the combinatorial characteristic
of binary ofﬂoading policies and resource optimization, we
propose a coordinate descent (CD)-based algorithm to opti-
mize the total energy consumption of all devices. The main
contributions of this work are summarized as follows.
• We consider a joint optimization framework for multi-
device edge intelligence systems where mobile devices
executing local inference jointly optimize the memory
frequency and computing frequency to reduce the energy
consumption. To this end, we characterize the impact of
joint memory frequency and computing frequency scaling
on DNN inference time. Speciﬁcally, the non-linear least
square method is applied based on real data to ﬁt the
inference time as a function of both memory frequency
and computing frequency. In addition, the power charac-
teristics of memory frequency and computing frequency
are investigated to obtain the energy consumption of
DNN inference.
• We formulate an optimization problem that involves the
joint optimization of memory frequency, computing fre-
quency, uplink bandwidth and ofﬂoading policy to mini-
mize the total energy consumption of all mobile devices,
with the given deadline constraint. The problem is a
mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem,
and the strong coupling of ofﬂoading policy and resource
allocation makes it difﬁcult to directly obtain the optimal
solution with acceptable complexity.
• We develop an efﬁcient decomposition-based solution al-
gorithm by exploiting the structure of the problem. First,
given the ofﬂoading policy, the problem is decomposed
into a local subproblem optimizing the memory frequency
and computing frequency, and an edge subproblem opti-
mizing the uplink bandwidth. Then, the local subproblem
is equivalently transformed into a GP problem, and the
optimal solution can be derived. The optimal bandwidth
allocation can be derived due to the convexity of the edge
subproblem. Finally, we propose a CD-based algorithm
to optimize the original ofﬂoading policy and obtain a
local optimum for the original problem.
• Based on real data, we evaluate the performance of our
proposed algorithm under different parameter settings.
Speciﬁcally, we compare the energy consumption, infer-
ence time, memory frequency and computing frequency
of devices among our proposed solution, memory-only
solution and computing-only solution for local inference.
In addition, our proposed algorithm achieves near-optimal
performance for the overall problem and signiﬁcantly
outperforms the other benchmark policies. Finally, the
impact of deadline and bandwidth on memory frequency
and computing frequency in a speciﬁc case is given to
exhibit the tradeoff between communication and mem-
ory/computing resources.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section
II gives an overview of related work. Section III describes the
system model and problem formulation. Section IV provides a
detailed solution to the original problem. Section V shows the
simulation results to evaluate the proposed algorithm. Finally,
Section VI concludes this work.
II. RELATED WORK
In this section, we review the existing literature on com-
putation ofﬂoading, management and optimization of memory
resources, and energy-efﬁcient DNN inference.
A. Computation Ofﬂoading
Extensive studies have focused on the computation ofﬂoad-
ing in MEC and edge intelligence systems, addressing how to
allocate computing and communication resources and make


--- Page 3 ---
3
ofﬂoading decisions. The binary ofﬂoading paradigm allows
mobile devices to either ofﬂoad tasks to the MEC server or
execute local computation [31], [32]. In [31], a robust task
ofﬂoading and resource allocation algorithm is proposed to
address the imperfect computing capacity information. In [32],
a distributed online algorithm is proposed to minimize the
energy consumption of ground devices in the aerial-based
MEC system. To further reduce the energy consumption of
computation and transmission, the partial ofﬂoading scheme
combined with the DVFS technique has been studied [12],
[13], [15], [16]. In [12], the authors consider an edge-device
cooperation system, where devices optimize the computing
frequency based on DVFS and ofﬂoading decisions while the
edge server executes batch processing to minimize the total
energy consumption. In [13], the authors propose a robust
DNN partitioning and resource allocation algorithm to reduce
the energy consumption of mobile devices with probabilistic
guarantees on deadlines. In [15], a deep reinforcement learn-
ing (DRL) method is proposed to optimize the computation
ofﬂoading ratio and computing frequency to minimize the
energy consumption for real-time IoT applications. In [16],
a diffusion-based DRL algorithm is proposed to optimize
the DNN partitioning policies, computation ofﬂoading and
computing resource allocation in vehicular networks. However,
these studies ignore the impact of memory resources on the
latency and energy consumption of mobile devices.
B. Management and Optimization of Memory Resources
A few studies have focused on memory footprint manage-
ment and data-movement reduction [20], [21], [22], [33], as
well as memory frequency optimization [24], [25], [34], [35],
[36]. Speciﬁcally, Smart-Zone [20] designs a memory-efﬁcient
management scheme for TrustZone-enabled IoT devices that
dynamically optimizes secure and shared memory allocation
to enable efﬁcient and secure DNN inference. SwapNet [21]
designs a zero-copy block swapping and model assembly
mechanism to eliminate redundant memory operations for
efﬁcient DNN inference on edge devices with limited memory
budgets. FlexNN [22] adaptively manages and optimizes mem-
ory utilization to achieve latency-memory tradeoffs. FlashAt-
tention [33] introduces an IO-aware attention with tiling and
recomputation to reduce GPU memory accesses and latency.
As for memory frequency, [24] characterizes a ﬁne-grained
model to estimate the memory access latency with memory
and computing frequency scaling. [34] decouples the GPU
power consumption into computing and memory frequency
domains, and presents models to predict the power consump-
tion for various applications. [35] combines dynamic memory
frequency scaling and DRAM low-power states to improve
the energy consumption. [36] proposes a new multi-domain
(e.g., compute, I/O, memory) power management technique
to improve the energy efﬁciency of mobile System on Chip
(SoC) with the ﬁne-grained DVFS technique. However, it is
difﬁcult to directly apply the ﬁne-grained models proposed
by [24], [34] and [35] for memory frequency optimization
in DNN inference. Although [25] jointly optimizes DVFS
and computation ofﬂoading ratio, the function relationship
among the inference time, memory frequency and computing
frequency is not characterized.
C. Energy-Efﬁcient DNN Inference
Recent studies have investigated energy-efﬁcient DNN in-
ference from different perspectives. For on-device or edge
inference, E4 [37] achieves energy-efﬁcient DNN inference
by integrating early exit with DVFS, where an attention-
based module adaptively determines the DNN exit point and a
proﬁler optimizes CPU/GPU frequencies for the layers before
the selected exit point. Squeezer [38] focuses on efﬁcient
multi-DNN inference for edge video analytics through cross-
model scheduling, where balanced operator grouping reduces
scheduling complexity and a kernel scheduler coordinates par-
allel kernel execution to fully utilize the computing resources.
For collaborative edge-cloud computing scenarios, [39] pro-
poses a hybrid resource reserving and expansion scheme,
where edge resources are managed locally and cloud resources
are utilized for expansion to improve the system efﬁciency.
[40] combines early exit with DNN partitioning in device-edge
collaboration, where DNN branch selection, partitioning point
selection, computing and communication resource allocation
are jointly optimized to reduce the energy consumption while
satisfying the accuracy requirements. PIDC [41] proposes a
padding-aware framework that jointly optimizes DNN par-
titioning and padding data exchange among IoT devices to
minimize inference latency. In addition, [25] combines the
memory frequency scaling with edge-cloud cooperation, and
designs a DRL algorithm that co-optimizes DVFS and the
ofﬂoading ratio to reduce the end-to-end latency and energy
consumption.
Different from the existing work, this paper mainly in-
vestigates the impact of jointly adjusting memory frequency
and computing frequency on DNN inference. We develop
proﬁling-based models to characterize the impact of these
two frequencies on both inference time and energy consump-
tion. These models are incorporated into the proposed frame-
work that jointly optimizes memory frequency, computing
frequency, uplink bandwidth and ofﬂoading policy to minimize
the total energy consumption of all mobile devices under the
deadline constraint. Unlike the DRL-based method in [25],
the proposed joint optimization scheme exploits the analytical
structure of the formulated problem and provides tractable
solutions to the decomposed subproblems.
III. SYSTEM MODEL AND PROBLEM FORMULATION
A. Network Model
As shown in Fig. 2, we consider an edge intelligence system
consisting of N mobile devices, denoted by the set N ≜
{1, . . ., N}, and a wireless edge node integrated with an MEC
server. Each mobile device deploys pre-trained DNNs (e.g.,
ResNet [28], VGG [29], or ViT [30]) to execute inference tasks
(e.g., image recognition). We assume that the MEC server
adopts a pre-conﬁgured resource allocation architecture, where
an independent virtual machine (VM) is allocated to each
device [42]. Each VM stores the corresponding DNN models
and executes the inference task ofﬂoaded by the associated

device in parallel. The computing and memory frequencies
of each VM are set to the maximum values.1 The Frequency
Division Multiple Access (FDMA) technique is adopted [43],
[44], where the interference between mobile devices can be
ignored.2 The binary ofﬂoading policy xn ∈{0, 1}, ∀n ∈N
is used, which means that each mobile device can process
its inference task locally (xn = 0) or ofﬂoad its task to
the corresponding VM for remote processing (xn = 1). For
example, device 1 and device 2 set to xn = 1 ofﬂoad their
inference tasks to VM 1 and VM 2 with stronger processing
capacities, while device 3 set to xn = 0 completes its task
locally.
In this work, the joint optimization of memory frequency
and computing frequency for mobile devices is considered.
Speciﬁcally, the inference process can be generally divided
into three steps. ❶The DNN model parameters are ﬁrst loaded
into the memory (e.g., DRAM, SRAM). ❷When performing
the forward computation layer by layer, GPU kernels access
the required input data and parameters from memory, perform
the computation, and store the intermediate outputs back to
memory as the inputs of subsequent layers. ❸Finally, the
forward computation is completed and the inference result is

determine the memory access and forward computation time,
respectively. Since both frequency domains contribute to the
overall inference time and energy consumption, mobile devices
executing local inference should jointly optimize these two
frequencies to reduce the energy consumption. The major

B. Inference Time and Energy Consumption
In most existing studies, the inference time is modeled as
the ratio between the required computation workload (e.g.,
CPU cycles or ﬂoating-point operations) and the processing
capability [11], [45]. However, this formulation fails to account
for the impact of memory frequency, which plays a crucial
role in determining the inference time. To characterize the
impact of joint memory frequency and computing frequency
scaling, we measure the average inference time of several
representative DNNs on different hardware platforms under
various combinations of memory frequency and computing
frequency, as shown in Fig. 3. Speciﬁcally, ResNet152 and
Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) [46] are deployed on

Jetson TX1 to execute inference using the CIFAR-100 and

[48] are evaluated on Jetson Orin Nano and Jetson Orin NX
using the CIFAR-100 and ImageNet [49] datasets, respectively.
For each memory and computing frequency conﬁguration, we
perform 10 warm-up runs and calculate the average inference
time over the same 100 samples. Based on the real data, we use
the non-linear least square method to characterize the function
relationship between inference time and these two frequencies,
which is illustrated by the ﬁtting surface.
Let fn,m and fn,c denote the memory frequency and com-
puting frequency of mobile device n, respectively. Then, the
local inference time of mobile device n is characterized by

where an, bn, cn and dn are positive coefﬁcients relevant to the
hardware, the type of DNNs, etc. The ﬁtting parameters and
accuracy metrics are summarized in Table II. We analyze the
mean squared error (MSE), root mean squared error (RMSE),
mean absolute error (MAE), mean absolute percentage error
(MAPE) and R-squared (R2) to provide a more comprehensive
evaluation of the ﬁtting accuracy. The ﬁtted model achieves
small MSE, RMSE, MAE and MAPE values, while R2 is
larger than 0.99 in most cases, which further indicates the
effectiveness of this model.3 Parameters an and bn reﬂect the
impact of memory frequency, while cn and dn reﬂect the im-
pact of computing frequency. It is observed that the inference
time exhibits a signiﬁcant decrease as the memory frequency
increases, verifying the impact of memory frequency scaling.
In addition, when the memory frequency is higher, there is
a larger decrease in the inference time with the increase of
computing frequency. However, with extremely low memory
frequency, increasing the computing frequency cannot lead to
a distinct effect. This is because during DNN inference, GPUs
not only perform arithmetic operations but also frequently ac-
cess model parameters, input/output feature maps and interme-
diate activations. When the memory frequency is low, memory
access becomes the major bottleneck, and the computing units
may stall while waiting for the required data. In this case,
increasing the computing frequency alone cannot effectively

reduce the inference latency. Optimizing only the computing
frequency while keeping the memory frequency ﬁxed may lead
to a suboptimal energy-latency tradeoff, especially when the
DNN inference workload is memory-bound. This observation
further supports the motivation of this work, and it is necessary
to jointly consider the memory frequency and computing
frequency in the proposed optimization framework.
Based on the above analysis, the local inference time is
formulated as a function related to both memory frequency and
computing frequency. Moreover, it is essential to investigate
the power characteristics associated with these two frequen-
cies in order to accurately characterize the overall energy
consumption. The dynamic power consumption is typically
modeled as P = κf 3, where κ and f denote the energy
coefﬁcient and computing frequency, respectively [50], [51].
However, the total power consumption should account for not
only the computing frequency domain, but also the memory
frequency domain [34]. To this end, we obtain the power
consumption under different settings of memory frequency
and computing frequency on two devices using the NVIDIA
Tegrastats toolkit [52], as illustrated in Fig. 4 and Fig. 5.
Denote κn,m and κn,c as the energy coefﬁcients for memory
frequency and computing frequency, respectively. Then, the
power consumption of mobile device n is modeled as

form model, since it has been widely adopted as a tractable approximation of
dynamic power consumption. However, the proposed optimization framework
and method do not rely on a strict cubic power model.

6
and 1.4 × 10−3 W2, respectively. For Jetson Orin Nano, the
corresponding MSEs are 1.3 × 10−4 W2 and 1.1 × 10−4 W2,
respectively. The MSEs are extremely small and R2 is larger
than 0.95, verifying the effectiveness of our ﬁtted power
model. In addition, it is observed that the static power of
memory is larger than that of computing, while the dynamic
power presents an opposite result. The different latency and
power consumption characteristics of memory and computing
frequency directly determine the energy consumption of local
inference for mobile device n, which is given by

For mobile devices executing edge inference, the energy
consumption of transmission should be considered. Denote
Bn as the uplink bandwidth allocated to mobile device n for
ofﬂoading the inference task, where Bn is constrained by the
total bandwidth B (i.e., P
n∈N Bn ≤B, Bn ≥0). Then, the
spectral efﬁciency of the wireless link between the edge node
and mobile device n is given by ηn = log2(1 + pnhn
BnN0 ), where
pn is the transmission power of device n, hn is the channel
gain between device n and the edge node, and N0 is the power
spectral density of the noise. Therefore, the transmission time
of device n for ofﬂoading its task to the edge node is

, ∀n ∈N,

consumption of mobile device n is given by

, ∀n ∈N.

Based on the assumptions in the last subsection, for a given
DNN model and VM conﬁguration, the edge inference time
of device n can be measured through ofﬂine proﬁling and
treated as a constant, denoted by tE
n. Given that the size of the
inference result is usually much smaller than the raw data and
the edge node possesses signiﬁcantly high transmission power
and bandwidth, the result feedback delay from the edge node
to mobile devices is ignored [31], [53].
C. Problem Formulation
Based on the above analysis, the energy consumption of
mobile device n is given by
En = (1 −xn) eL
n + xneO
n , ∀n ∈N,
(6)
and the corresponding inference time of mobile device n is
Tn = (1 −xn) tL
n + xn
␀tO


, ∀n ∈N.
(7)
Due to the real-time demand for DNN inference, the infer-
ence time should satisfy the deadline constraint, i.e., Tn ≤
Dn, ∀n ∈N, where Dn is the inference task deadline of
mobile device n. The objective is to minimize the total energy
consumption of mobile devices by jointly optimizing the
binary ofﬂoading policy x ≜{xn}n∈N , memory frequency
fM ≜{fn,m}n∈N , computing frequency fC ≜{fn,c}n∈N ,
and uplink bandwidth b ≜{Bn}n∈N , while the deadline
constraint should be satisﬁed. Therefore, the optimization
problem is formulated as
min
x,b,fM,fC
X
n∈N
En
(8a)
s.t. Tn ≤Dn, ∀n ∈N,
(8b)
fn,m ∈[fn,min, fn,max] , ∀n ∈N,
(8c)
fn,c ∈[Fn,min, Fn,max] , ∀n ∈N,
(8d)
X
n∈N
xnBn ≤B,
(8e)
xn ∈{0, 1}, ∀n ∈N,
(8f)
Bn ≥0, ∀n ∈N,
(8g)
where (8b) represents the deadline constraint of inference
time, (8c) and (8d) correspond to the memory frequency and
computing frequency constraints, (8e) and (8g) give the uplink
bandwidth constraint, and (8f) indicates the ofﬂoading policy
constraint. The objective function is generally non-convex,
and the introduction of memory frequency increases the com-
plexity of problem (8). In addition, even when the memory
frequency is given, problem (8) is still an MINLP problem,
which is generally NP-hard. To solve this problem, we ﬁrst
assume that the ofﬂoading policy is given and derive the
optimal solutions to the two subproblems. Then, we propose a
low-complexity algorithm to solve the original problem. The
detailed solutions are given in Section IV.
IV. JOINT OPTIMIZATION OF MEMORY FREQUENCY,
COMPUTING FREQUENCY AND OFFLOADING
In this section, we use a decoupling method to solve the
optimization problem (8). We ﬁrst assume that the ofﬂoading
policy is given, and derive two independent subproblems to
optimize the energy consumption of local inference and task
ofﬂoading. Then, the local subproblem (i.e., optimization of
memory frequency and computing frequency) is transformed
into an equivalent GP problem, and the optimal solution is
obtained. Meanwhile, since the edge subproblem (i.e., uplink
bandwidth allocation) is a convex optimization problem, the
optimal solution can be obtained. Finally, an efﬁcient CD
algorithm is proposed to optimize the ofﬂoading policy.
A. Problem Decomposition and Overview
Problem (8) can be decomposed into independent sub-
problems with separate optimization variables and constraints,
which are relatively easy to solve. First, with the given
ofﬂoading policy, the local subproblem is given as follows
min

(9b)

to the total energy consumption of all mobile devices that
execute local inference. Meanwhile, with the given ofﬂoading
policy, the edge subproblem is expressed as

Since the objective function and constraints of problem (15)
are all convex, problem (15) is a standard convex optimization
problem [13], [57], and the optimal bandwidth allocation
can be solved with an interior-point algorithm. The compu-
tational complexity of solving problem (15) for each iteration
is O
␀V2|N1|2
, and the number of iterations for the IPM
algorithm is O(√V2 log(1/ǫ)), where V2 = 2|N1| + 1 and
ǫ represent the number of constraints and the convergence ac-
curacy, respectively [56]. Therefore, the overall computational
complexity of solving problem (15) is O(|N1|3.5 log(1/ǫ)).
The overall procedure for solving problem (8) with the
given ofﬂoading policy is presented in Algorithm 1. The
optimal solution to problem (12) is derived by solving problem
(14) with relatively low computational complexity, while the
optimal bandwidth is derived by solving problem (15). There-
fore, Algorithm 1 can obtain the optimal memory frequency,
computing frequency and bandwidth allocation under a given
ofﬂoading policy in polynomial time complexity.
D. Task Ofﬂoading
An efﬁcient CD algorithm is used to optimize the ofﬂoading
policy x = (x1, . . . , xN). The CD algorithm optimizes x along
the descent direction of only one variable xi each time to
ﬁnd a local minimum [58]. Speciﬁcally, the CD algorithm ﬁrst
starts from a feasible ofﬂoading policy x(0) randomly, where
each element takes a value of either 0 or 1. Denote x(l−1)
as the binary ofﬂoading policy in the (l −1)th iteration, l =
1, 2, · · · . Correspondingly, denote V

Proposition 1: Algorithm 2 converges in a ﬁnite number of
iterations and returns a local optimum of problem (8).

than 2N. Moreover, Algorithm 2 cannot revisit any previously
visited ofﬂoading policy, because the objective value strictly
decreases after each accepted update. Therefore, Algorithm
2 must terminate within a ﬁnite number of iterations. When

reduce the objective value. Therefore, the obtained ofﬂoading
policy is a local optimum. Since Algorithm 1 provides the
optimal resource allocation for the obtained ofﬂoading policy,
Algorithm 2 returns a local optimum of problem (8).
Finally, we analyze the computational complexity of Algo-
rithm 2. Since each iteration of the CD algorithm needs to
run Algorithm 1 N times, the computational complexity of
Algorithm 2 depends on Algorithm 1. If Algorithm 2 requires
L iterations to converge, the overall computational complexity
of Algorithm 2 is O(LN 4.5 log(1/ǫ)).
V. SIMULATION RESULTS
In this section, we ﬁrst present the simulation setting. Then,
we illustrate and analyze the performance of our proposed
solution for local inference. Next, we empirically evaluate the
convergence of Algorithm 2, and give the performance eval-
uation under different parameter settings. Finally, we analyze
the impact of deadline and bandwidth on the optimization of
memory frequency and computing frequency in a speciﬁc case.
A. Simulation Setting
We consider an edge intelligence system similar to [31],
where the edge node is at the center of a 400 m × 400 m
square area, and all mobile devices are randomly placed within
the area. The path loss (in dB) between mobile device n and
the edge node is characterized as PL = 38 + 30 log10 rn [59],
where rn (in meters) is the distance between mobile device
n and the edge node. The transmission power is 1 W, and
the noise power spectral density is N0 = −174 dBm/Hz [31],
[60].
To evaluate the proposed algorithm, we conduct experi-
ments on three hardware platforms with diverse DNN models.
Speciﬁcally, ResNet152 [28], VGG19 [29] and LSTM [46]
are deployed on Jetson TX1 and evaluated on the CIFAR-100
and UCI HAR datasets. ResNet152 and ViT-B/16 [30] are
deployed on Jetson Orin Nano for inference on the CIFAR-
100 dataset. Swin-B [48] and GNN [61] are deployed on
Jetson Orin NX and evaluated on the ImageNet and ogbn-arxiv
datasets from the Open Graph Benchmark (OGB) [62]. Each
VM is conﬁgured with an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4080. The
corresponding parameters and conﬁgurations are summarized
in Table III.
B. Comparison for Local Inference
We ﬁrst compare the performance of our proposed solution
with two benchmark methods under different deadlines for
local inference. Speciﬁcally, the memory-only solution is given
as a benchmark, which ﬁxes the computing frequency to the
maximum value and only optimizes the memory frequency.
The computing-only solution is provided as another bench-
mark, which ﬁxes the memory frequency to the maximum
value and only optimizes the computing frequency.
Fig. 7 presents the energy consumption of one mobile device
executing local inference for our proposed solution, memory-
only solution and computing-only solution. Based on the anal-
ysis in Section IV, our proposed solution is optimal, which can
be derived by solving the equivalent GP problem and performs
better than the other two benchmark solutions for the energy
consumption. In Fig. 7(a) and Fig. 7(c), the performance gap
is relatively small with a small deadline. As the deadline
increases, our proposed solution can further reduce the energy
consumption, while the reductions achieved by the memory-
only and computing-only solutions are limited. Speciﬁcally,
compared with the memory-only and computing-only solu-
tions, our proposed solution can reduce the energy consump-
tion by 12.6% and 9.0% with Dn = 280 ms for ResNet152
on Jetson TX1, respectively. Compared with the memory-only
and computing-only solutions, the proposed solution reduces
the energy consumption by 9.3% and 17.2% with Dn = 150
ms for Swin-B on Jetson Orin NX, respectively. However,
in Fig. 7(b), the energy consumption of our proposed solu-
tion does not signiﬁcantly decrease with the deadline, where
the corresponding performance gaps from the memory-only
and computing-only solutions are only 1.7% and 5.6% with
Dn = 65 ms for ViT-B/16 on Jetson Orin Nano, respectively.
For the memory-only and computing-only solutions with larger
deadlines, the energy consumption remains constant because
the optimization of memory/computing frequency is limited
when the computing/memory frequency is set to the maximum.
In conclusion, by jointly optimizing the memory frequency
and computing frequency, the energy consumption of local
inference can be further reduced.
Fig. 8 illustrates the actual inference time of three solutions
under different deadlines. In Fig. 8(a) and Fig. 8(c), although
the inference time of our proposed solution is equal to that of
the computing-only solution with a relatively small deadline,
their energy consumption differs due to distinct choices of
memory frequency and computing frequency. As the deadline
increases, the inference time of our proposed solution be-
comes larger than that of the memory-only or computing-only
solution, indicating that our proposed solution fully exploits
the available deadline to reduce the energy consumption of
local inference. Moreover, the inference time of our proposed
solution remains constant when the deadline further increases,

which is attributed to the complicated and non-monotonic
objective function in problem (12). In addition, the difference
among the three solutions in Fig. 8(b) is relatively small, which
is consistent with the results shown in Fig. 7(b).
To further analyze the difference among the three solutions,
we evaluate the speciﬁc values of memory frequency and
computing frequency under different deadline constraints, as
shown in Fig. 9. As the deadline increases, the memory
frequency and computing frequency derived by our proposed
solution can be reduced. With a larger deadline, it is observed
that our proposed solution obtains smaller memory frequencies
and computing frequencies than the other two benchmark
methods, leading to smaller energy consumption. In Fig. 9(a)
and Fig. 9(c), the frequency gap is much larger, which is con-
sistent with the performance gain shown in Fig. 7(a) and Fig.
7(c). The computing frequency gap among the three solutions
is not signiﬁcantly large in Fig. 9(b), since the parameters cn
and dn for Jetson Orin Nano are relatively small. In summary,
the memory frequency and computing frequency should be
properly optimized to balance the inference time and energy
consumption. Although the benchmark methods reduce the
inference time by increasing the computing frequency and
memory frequency, this latency reduction is not sufﬁcient to
compensate for the increased power consumption, resulting in
higher overall energy consumption. Our proposed solution can
provide a more appropriate selection for the memory frequency
and computing frequency to reduce the energy consumption
of local inference.

C. Convergence of Algorithm 2
Fig. 10 presents the average number of iterations for Al-
gorithm 2 under various numbers of devices. Although the
number of iterations required for convergence is difﬁcult to
characterize analytically, the proposed CD-based algorithm
empirically converges within a few iterations, even when the
network scale increases to N = 36. Moreover, the average
numbers of iterations required for the three DNN models
are generally comparable. In addition, the average number of
iterations required by Algorithm 2 increases marginally with
the number of devices, which demonstrates the scalability and
efﬁciency of the proposed algorithm.
D. Performance Evaluation of Algorithm 2
In this subsection, we evaluate the energy consumption
performance of Algorithm 2 under various parameter settings.
Speciﬁcally, we consider the following ﬁve benchmark policies
for performance comparison:
• Optimal policy: the optimal memory frequency, comput-
ing frequency and bandwidth are obtained by Algorithm
1, and the optimal ofﬂoading policy is determined by
exhaustive search.
• Computing-only policy [13]: only the computing fre-
quency is optimized in the local subproblem, and the CD
algorithm is used to determine the ofﬂoading policy.
• No-scaling policy: the memory frequency and computing
frequency are set to the maximum values and not opti-
mized in the local subproblem, and the CD algorithm is
used to determine the ofﬂoading policy.
• DRL-based policy [25]: the DQN is adopted to optimize
the memory frequency, computing frequency and ofﬂoad-
ing policy, and the bandwidth allocation is obtained by
the convex optimization method.
• Random policy: the optimal memory frequency, comput-
ing frequency and bandwidth are obtained by Algorithm
1, and the ofﬂoading policy is given randomly.
1) Impact of Device Numbers: In Fig. 11(a), Fig. 12(a) and
Fig. 13(a), we compare the performance of different policies
under various numbers of devices. It is observed that the
average energy consumption increases with the number of
devices when the deadline and communication resources are
given. As expected, the average energy consumption of the
optimal policy is the lowest, which provides a lower bound
for other policies. When the number of devices is small
(i.e., N ≤8), our proposed algorithm can almost achieve
the optimal performance. For example, when the number of
devices N = 8, our proposed algorithm achieves the optimal
energy consumption in Fig. 11(a), while the performance gap
between the optimal policy and our proposed algorithm is only
1.4% in Fig. 12(a). In this case, the communication resources
are sufﬁcient and almost all mobile devices can ofﬂoad their
tasks to the edge server. As the number of devices increases,
the performance of our proposed algorithm is still close to the
optimal policy, and signiﬁcantly outperforms other benchmark
policies. This is because the communication resources are
limited to support task ofﬂoading for all mobile devices,
and some devices must execute local inference to meet the
deadline constraint, leading to the increase of average energy
consumption and performance gap.
Speciﬁcally, for ResNet152, ViT-B/16 and Swin-B, the per-
formance gap between our proposed algorithm and the optimal
policy is no more than 6.4%, 1.5% and 9.3%, respectively.
Compared with the computing-only policy, our proposed al-
gorithm can reduce the average energy consumption by up
to 8.0%, 4.8% and 15.6%, respectively, which veriﬁes the
beneﬁt of jointly optimizing memory frequency and computing
frequency. The average energy consumption of no-scaling
policy is larger than that of computing-only policy, since the
no-scaling policy sets both memory frequency and computing
frequency to the maximum values during local inference.
Compared with the DRL-based policy, the proposed algorithm
achieves lower energy consumption with average reductions
of 8.2%, 10.2% and 16.0%, respectively. This is because
the DRL-based policy learns the ofﬂoading and frequency
decisions from sampled interactions and does not exploit the
analytical structure of the problem. In fact, the learned policy
is not stable and may violate the given deadline constraint.
The random policy performs the worst in most cases because
it randomly determines the ofﬂoading decision and thus cannot
effectively exploit the available communication resources.
2) Impact of Deadline: In Fig. 7, we have observed the im-
pact of deadline on the energy consumption of local inference.
To further investigate the impact of deadline on the average
energy consumption per device in the multi-device case, we
compare the performance of ﬁve policies under different
deadlines, as shown in Fig. 11(b), Fig. 12(b) and Fig. 13(b).
As the deadline increases, the average energy consumption
shows a decreasing trend. Increasing the deadline can provide
more opportunities for devices to ofﬂoad their inference tasks
and reduce the energy consumption. The performance gap
between our proposed algorithm and the optimal policy is no
more than 6.0%, 5.6% and 8.0% for ResNet152, ViT-B/16
and Swin-B, respectively. Moreover, our proposed algorithm
can achieve near-optimal performance when the deadline is
large enough, since more devices ofﬂoad their tasks and the
difference only arises from the local inference. Compared with
the computing-only policy, our proposed algorithm can reduce
the average energy consumption by at most 5.8%, 6.4% and
15.4%, respectively. Compared with the DRL-based policy,

3) Impact of Bandwidth: In Fig. 11(c), Fig. 12(c) and Fig.
13(c), the impact of bandwidth on average energy consumption
for different policies is presented. Similar to the impact of
deadline, increasing the bandwidth can signiﬁcantly reduce
the average energy consumption. This is because with more
bandwidth resources, there are more devices ofﬂoading tasks
to the edge node, and the energy consumption of communi-
cation is much smaller than that of executing local inference.
For ResNet152, ViT-B/16 and Swin-B, the maximum perfor-
mance gap between our proposed algorithm and the optimal
policy is 3.6%, 1.2% and 7.0%, respectively. In addition, our
proposed algorithm outperforms the computing-only policy by
up to 7.1%, 4.1% and 16.1%, respectively, achieved under
relatively small bandwidth resources (i.e., B = 6 MHz in
Fig. 11(c), B = 20 MHz in Fig. 12(c) and B = 6 MHz
in Fig. 13(c)). Another observation is that both our proposed
algorithm and the computing-only policy achieve near-optimal

performance when the bandwidth resources are abundant (e.g.,
B = 14 MHz in Fig. 11(c)), since almost all devices select
to ofﬂoad inference tasks in this case. Compared with the
DRL-based policy, the proposed algorithm can reduce the
energy consumption by 11.0%, 13.2% and 12.3% on aver-
age, respectively. In conclusion, our proposed algorithm can
signiﬁcantly reduce the average energy consumption by jointly
optimizing the memory frequency, computing frequency and
the allocation of bandwidth resources.
4) Ablation Studies: The above results have shown the
advantage of jointly optimizing memory frequency and com-
puting frequency by comparing with several benchmark meth-
ods. To further verify the effect for other types of DNNs,
we conduct ablation studies for LSTM on Jetson TX1 and
GNN on Jetson Orin NX, and the results are shown in Table
IV and Table V, respectively. In the computing-only policy,
only the computing frequency is optimized while the memory
frequency is ﬁxed at the maximum value. In the memory-
only policy, only the memory frequency is optimized while
the computing frequency is ﬁxed at the maximum value.
The discrete-points policy searches over discrete memory and
computing frequency conﬁgurations to obtain the appropriate
combination, while the proposed method jointly optimizes
both memory frequency and computing frequency in a con-
tinuous manner. The beneﬁt of jointly optimizing memory
frequency and computing frequency is highly dependent on
the model architecture and hardware platform. For LSTM
on Jetson TX1, the computing-only policy achieves energy
consumption close to that of the proposed method, while the
memory-only policy results in consistently higher energy con-
sumption. This indicates that the optimal memory frequency
is close to the maximum value. The ﬁtting parameters also
imply that the inference time of LSTM is more sensitive
to memory frequency. For GNN on Jetson Orin NX, the
memory-only policy signiﬁcantly outperforms the computing-
only policy and achieves almost the same performance as
the proposed method, since the optimal computing frequency
is pushed to the maximum value. It is observed that the
proposed continuous frequency optimization and the discrete-
points policy achieve close energy consumption. This is
because when the available discrete frequency points are
sufﬁciently dense and close to the continuous optimum, the

with N = 8 mobile devices, where devices 1 to 4 use the

Fig. 15. Memory frequency and computing frequency solved by
Algorithm 2 under different bandwidth resources in a speciﬁc case.
Jetson TX1 conﬁguration and the remaining devices use the
Jetson Orin Nano conﬁguration. VGG19 and ResNet152 are
deployed on Jetson TX1 and Jetson Orin Nano, respectively,
and the bandwidth is set to B = 4 MHz. We derive the
memory frequency and computing frequency based on Al-
gorithm 2, and the results are shown in Fig. 14(a) and Fig.
14(b). As the deadline increases, the memory frequencies and
computing frequencies of devices 2 and 3 show a decreasing
trend. When the deadline is set to Dn = 0.21 s, device 2
ofﬂoads its inference task, leading to the minimum memory
frequency and computing frequency. On the one hand, increas-
ing the deadline may lead to smaller memory frequencies and
computing frequencies for energy-efﬁcient DNN inference. On
the other hand, devices have more opportunities to ofﬂoad
their inference tasks to reduce the energy consumption. With
the limited bandwidth resources, devices 5 to 8 execute local
inference. This is because the energy consumption of local
inference on Jetson Orin Nano is smaller than that of Jetson
TX1. In addition, the memory frequencies and computing
frequencies of devices 5 to 8 do not decrease with the deadline,
since the optimal energy consumption has been achieved.
Finally, we analyze the impact of bandwidth on memory fre-
quency and computing frequency in the multi-device case. We
consider the same scenario with N = 8 mobile devices, where
the deadline is set to Dn = 0.16 s. The results are shown
in Fig. 15(a) and Fig. 15(b), respectively. As the bandwidth
increases, there are more devices that can ofﬂoad inference
tasks, which leads to the decrease of memory frequency and
computing frequency. When the bandwidth is set to B = 22
MHz, all mobile devices ofﬂoad tasks to the edge node, and the
memory frequency and computing frequency are adjusted to
the minimum values. It can be observed that device 8 reduces
the memory frequency to the minimum when B = 8 MHz,
but increases the memory frequency when B = 10 MHz.
A similar phenomenon can be observed for device 7 when
B = 14 MHz and B = 16 MHz. This is because the system
can adaptively optimize the bandwidth resource allocation
to minimize the total energy consumption. In addition, the
computing frequencies for devices 5 to 8 do not change with
the bandwidth, since the computing frequency is scaled to
the minimum even when devices execute local inference. For
Jetson Orin Nano, the computing frequency range is relatively
small, and the adjustment of memory frequency plays a more
signiﬁcant role in the inference time and energy consumption
of DNN inference. In summary, Algorithm 2 can achieve
an excellent balance between communication resources and
memory/computing resources.
VI. CONCLUSION
In this paper, we investigated the joint optimization of
memory frequency, computing frequency, bandwidth alloca-
tion, and ofﬂoading in the multi-device edge intelligence
system. Motivated by the experiments that demonstrated the
impact of memory frequency scaling on latency and energy
consumption of DNN inference, we formulated an energy
minimization problem under the deadline constraint and solved
it through a decomposition approach. Our proposed algorithm
integrated GP-based frequency optimization, bandwidth allo-
cation with convex optimization, and a CD-based ofﬂoading
policy optimization. Extensive evaluations based on real data
were conducted under different parameter settings. The results
demonstrate that our proposed algorithm can reduce the aver-
age energy consumption by at most 8.0%, 6.4% and 16.1%
compared with the computing-only policy for ResNet152 on
Jetson TX1, ViT-B/16 on Jetson Orin Nano and Swin-B on
Jetson Orin NX, respectively, while the performance gaps from
the optimal policy are within 6.4%, 5.6% and 9.3%.
Finally, several promising directions remain for future work.
First, device mobility in practical edge intelligence systems
may introduce channel uncertainty caused by fading. There-
fore, extending the proposed framework to robust or chance-
constrained resource allocation under channel uncertainty is
an important direction. Second, when multiple devices share
the MEC server, resource contention and queueing delay may
make the edge inference time variable rather than constant.
This motivates the joint optimization of computing/memory
resources at both mobile devices and the MEC server. Third,
the proposed framework can be further extended to collab-
orative device-edge inference with DNN partitioning, where
the latency and energy consumption of memory/computing
frequency scaling should be characterized at the DNN block
level. The corresponding optimization problem would need
to jointly consider DNN partitioning, memory/computing fre-
quency scaling, and wireless bandwidth allocation.

Yunchu Han (S’24) received the B.E. degree from
the Department of Electronic Engineering, Tsinghua
University in 2023. He is currently pursuing the
Ph.D. degree with the Network Integration for Ubiq-
uitous Linkage and Broadband Laboratory, Depart-
ment of Electronic Engineering, Tsinghua Univer-
sity. His research interests include green edge intel-
ligence, efﬁcient inference, mobile edge computing
and wireless communication.
Zhaojun Nan (S’20-M’23) received the B.S. de-
gree in automation from Jiamusi University, Jiamusi,
China, in 2009, the M.S. degree in navigation, guid-
ance and control from Harbin Engineering Univer-
sity, Harbin, China, in 2012, and the Ph.D. degree
in information and communication engineering from
Chongqing University, Chongqing, China, in 2022.
From 2012 to 2017, he worked for Tianjin 712
Communication & Broadcasting Co., Ltd., Tianjin,
China. From 2022 to 2025, he was a Postdoctoral
Researcher with the Department of Electronic Engi-
neering, Tsinghua University, Beijing, China. He is currently with the School
of Electronics and Internet of Things, Chongqing Polytechnic University
of Electronic Technology, Chongqing, China. His research interests include
mobile edge intelligence, vehicular networks and autonomous driving, and
green wireless communications. He has served as a TPC member for IEEE
Globecom, ICC and WCNC.
Sheng Zhou (S’06-M’12) received the B.E. and
Ph.D. degrees in electronic engineering from Ts-
inghua University, Beijing, China, in 2005 and 2011,
respectively. In 2010, he was a Visiting Student
with the Wireless System Lab, Department of Elec-
trical Engineering, Stanford University, Stanford,
CA, USA. From 2014 to 2015, he was a Visiting
Researcher with Central Research Lab, Hitachi Ltd.,
Tokyo, Japan. He is currently an Associate Profes-
sor with the Department of Electronic Engineering,
Tsinghua University, Beijing, China. His research
interests include cross-layer design for multiple antenna systems, mobile edge
computing, vehicular networks, and green wireless communications. He was
the recipient of the IEEE ComSoc Asia-Paciﬁc Board Outstanding Young
Researcher Award in 2017, and IEEE ComSoc Wireless Communications
Technical Committee Outstanding Young Researcher Award in 2020.
Zhisheng Niu (M’98-SM’99-F’12) graduated from
Beijing Jiaotong University, China, in 1985, and
got his M.E. and D.E. degrees from Toyohashi
University of Technology, Japan, in 1989 and 1992,
respectively. From 1992 to 1994, he worked for
Fujitsu Laboratories Ltd., Japan, and in 1994 joined
with Tsinghua University, Beijing, China, where he
is now a Professor at the Department of Electronic
Engineering. His major research interests include
queueing theory, trafﬁc engineering, mobile Internet,
radio resource management of wireless networks,
and green communication and networks.
Dr. Niu has been serving IEEE Communications Society since 2000 as
Chair of Beijing Chapter (2000-2008), Director of Asia-Paciﬁc Board (2008-
2009), Director for Conference Publications (2010-2011), Chair of Emerging
Technologies Committee (2014-2015), Director for Online Contents (2018-
2019) and the Editor-in-Chief of IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON GREEN COM-
MUNICATIONS AND NETWORKING (2020-2022). He received the Best Paper
Award of Asia-Paciﬁc Board in 2013, Distinguished Technical Achievement
Recognition Award of Green Communications and Computing Technical
Committee in 2018, and Harold Sobol Award for Exemplary Service to
Meetings & Conferences in 2019, all from the IEEE Communications Society.
He was selected as a distinguished lecturer of IEEE Communications Society
(2012-2015) as well as IEEE Vehicular Technologies Society (2014-2018).
He is a fellow of both IEEE and IEICE.
